title: Linux & Operating Systems
description: Follow 25 lessons from Linux paths, shell arguments and permission bits to process lifetimes, memory, resource limits, containers and incident diagnosis. Includes portable child-process tests and an optional Windows-to-WSL observation guide.
level: Foundations → intermediate practice with optional systems labs
prerequisites: Comfort creating files and opening a terminal.
Python functions, lists, exceptions and context managers for the optional portable kit; Python 3.14+ with no external packages. You can read the operating-system lessons without running it.
Optional Linux observations require an existing disposable Linux/WSL environment.
outcomes: Observe paths, streams, identities and process statuses without modifying the host.
Explain resource lifetimes, shutdown and bounded child execution.
Diagnose a failure and distinguish modeled results from Linux observations.
setup: On Windows run the portable Python kit in PowerShell. For Linux-only commands, open your existing WSL distribution with wsl (if already installed), then run commands in that Linux Bash terminal. PowerShell and Bash syntax differ. Installing WSL is optional and outside this baseline.

If no Linux environment is installed, complete the portable kit first; keep Linux observation tasks marked unexecuted. If choosing WSL later, use the official Microsoft installation guide and a disposable user practice folder.
Download the practice bundle and extract its named folder.
Run the README baseline commands before attempting independent extensions.
No credentials, cloud accounts or administrator actions are required for the local baseline.
nextSteps: Complete the staged projects and explain failure evidence.
Cross-reference the existing Python, SQL Server, networking and Kubernetes paths where relevant.
Run optional platform integration separately and record actual versions and results.

lessons.title: 1. Meet the operating system
lessons.takeaway: An operating system coordinates hardware and programs.

sections.title: Kernel, shell and distribution
paragraphs: An operating system coordinates hardware and programs. The kernel mediates memory, CPU time, devices and system calls; user-space programs include shells, browsers and service managers. A Linux distribution combines the kernel with utilities and packages. A terminal displays interaction; a shell interprets commands.

sections.title: An importer's file read
paragraphs: Imagine a notebook importer opening a CSV. Its Python code requests a file read through a library; the kernel checks access and supplies bytes from the filesystem. A missing file is an operating-system error that the application should report, not proof that Python is broken.
sections.example:
# Run inside Linux or WSL, not PowerShell
uname -s
cat /etc/os-release
# Expect Linux and distribution-specific metadata.

sections.title: Host, guest and container kernels
paragraphs: A container normally shares its host kernel. A virtual machine has a guest kernel. Windows commands in PowerShell are not interchangeable with Bash syntax even when their names look alike.

exercise.prompt: Draw where Python, Bash and a filesystem driver belong. Explain how a container differs from a VM.
exercise.solution: Python and Bash run in user space. The filesystem driver participates in kernel-managed I/O. Containers share a kernel; a VM runs a guest kernel.
checks: Place Python and Bash in user space and the filesystem driver in kernel-managed I/O.
Distinguish a shared container kernel from a VM guest kernel.

quiz.question: A Python importer requests bytes from a file. Which component mediates access to the filesystem resource?
options: The kernel, reached through the application library call
Bash, even when Python was launched without a shell
A private kernel embedded in the Python interpreter
quiz.explanation: Python runs in user space and requests file access through library and system calls. The kernel mediates that access and coordinates the filesystem and device operations.

lessons.title: 2. Find your way through files
lessons.takeaway: An absolute Linux path starts at /.

sections.title: Absolute and relative paths
paragraphs: An absolute Linux path starts at `/`. A relative path starts at the process working directory. The home directory is a user-specific location; `~` is expanded by the shell. Case matters on typical Linux filesystems, so `Report.csv` and `report.csv` may be different names.

sections.title: A service launched from /
paragraphs: A service launched from `/` reads `./data.csv` there, even if the script is stored in `/home/learner/app`. Locate both the working directory and the configured data path before changing code. `..` moves to the parent; `.` names the current directory.
sections.example:
pwd
mkdir -p notebook-lab/input
cd notebook-lab
printf "id,name\n1,Asha\n" > input/sample.csv
ls -l input
# All changes stay in notebook-lab.

sections.title: Path resolution versus authorization
paragraphs: Resolving a path is not an authorization check. Symlinks can redirect lookup, and another process can change filesystem state between checking and opening a path.

exercise.prompt: From notebook-lab, explain input/sample.csv and ../notebook-lab/input/sample.csv. Predict what happens after cd input.
exercise.solution: Initially both identify the sample. After cd input, input/sample.csv looks for a nested input directory; sample.csv is the correct relative path.
checks: Resolve both supplied paths to the sample while in notebook-lab.
After cd input, identify sample.csv as the relative path and input/sample.csv as a nested lookup.

quiz.question: A service runs from / while its script lives in /home/learner/app. Where does ./data.csv resolve?
options: Under the service working directory /
Beside the script in /home/learner/app
Under the user home directory regardless of working directory
quiz.explanation: It resolves to /data.csv. A relative path starts from the process working directory, which is / here, regardless of where the script is stored.

lessons.title: 3. Read, copy and inspect safely
lessons.takeaway: Before modifying a file, inspect its name, contents and parent directory.

sections.title: Copies, moves and removals
paragraphs: Before modifying a file, inspect its name, contents and parent directory. cp copies, mv renames or moves, and rm removes directory entries. Shell wildcards can match more files than expected. Practice in a dedicated folder and use literal names for destructive operations.

sections.title: Comparing a backup copy
paragraphs: Copy the sample into `backup.csv`, compare the files and verify both exist before experimenting. A backup in the same filesystem helps against accidental edits but does not protect against a lost disk or corrupted account.
sections.example:
cp input/sample.csv backup.csv
cat backup.csv
wc -l backup.csv
# Expect 2 lines; inspect with ls before any removal.

sections.title: Overwrite and deletion boundaries
paragraphs: An overwrite can happen without a recycle-bin recovery path. Do not use recursive deletion against a computed or unreviewed directory. The lab needs no sudo and no changes to system directories.

exercise.prompt: Write a three-step checklist before overwriting backup.csv; distinguish local copy from recovery backup.
exercise.solution: Verify the target path, retain a separate prior version, and compare after writing. Recovery backup also needs independent storage and a restore check.
checks: Verify the target, retain a prior version and compare the result after overwriting.
Require independent storage and a restore check for recovery beyond a same-disk copy.

quiz.question: Before overwriting backup.csv, which sequence preserves recoverable evidence?
options: Verify the target, retain a separate prior version, then compare the written result
Overwrite first, then copy the new file as the prior version
Check only the filename because a same-disk backup covers disk failure
quiz.explanation: Check the exact target before writing, keep its previous contents separately, and compare the result afterward. Overwriting the only copy first leaves nothing to recover if the write is wrong.

lessons.title: 4. Arguments, quoting and expansion
lessons.takeaway: A command receives an argument vector.

sections.title: Arguments and shell expansion
paragraphs: A command receives an argument vector. Bash performs expansion before launching it: unquoted variables can undergo word splitting and filename expansion. Double quotes preserve spaces while allowing variable expansion; single quotes generally preserve literal text. User input should be data rather than shell source.

sections.title: A filename containing spaces
paragraphs: The filename `quarterly report.csv` contains a space. An unquoted variable can become two arguments; a quoted variable supplies one. A subprocess argument list avoids shell parsing altogether and is a better default for application code.
sections.example:
name="quarterly report.csv"
printf "%s\n" "$name"
# One line containing the complete name.
# Application equivalent: subprocess.run(["tool", name], shell=False)

sections.title: Quoting across languages
paragraphs: Quoting is shell-specific. Bash syntax does not secure SQL, HTML or another shell automatically. Avoid constructing a shell command from untrusted text and avoid eval for this exercise.

exercise.prompt: Explain why subprocess.run(["echo", name]) differs from joining strings into a shell command.
exercise.solution: The list preserves argument boundaries without invoking shell expansion. Joined shell source can interpret spaces, substitutions and operators.
checks: Explain that an argument list preserves a filename containing spaces as one argument.
Contrast shell parsing of substitutions and operators with passing those characters as data.

quiz.question: The filename is quarterly report.csv. Why pass it in a subprocess argument list with shell=False?
options: It remains one argument without shell expansion
The subprocess automatically removes spaces from the filename
The argument list applies Bash quoting in every operating system
quiz.explanation: With shell=False and an argument list, quarterly report.csv is passed as one filename. The shell does not split its space or interpret special characters in it.

lessons.title: 5. Follow standard input, output and errors
lessons.takeaway: Programs conventionally receive input on descriptor 0, write normal output on 1 and diagnostics on 2.

sections.title: Descriptors, pipes and redirects
paragraphs: Programs conventionally receive input on descriptor 0, write normal output on 1 and diagnostics on 2. A pipe connects one process output to another process input. Redirection sends a stream to a file. > replaces file contents; >> appends.

sections.title: Filtering stdout and stderr
paragraphs: A log filter may emit matching lines on stdout but write a missing-file message on stderr. Capturing stdout alone can hide the diagnosis. A pipeline transforms a stream, but a downstream success does not necessarily establish that all upstream stages succeeded.
sections.example:
printf "INFO ready\nERROR invalid row\n" | grep ERROR
# Expect ERROR invalid row
# Bash only:
set -o pipefail
false | cat
printf "status=%s\n" "$?"
# Expect status=1

sections.title: Pipeline status and parsers
paragraphs: Bash pipeline status normally follows the last command. `set -o pipefail` changes that rule. Binary data and CSV quoting require suitable parsers; a simple `grep` pipeline is not a CSV importer.

exercise.prompt: Design separate destinations for a report and diagnostic log. Explain why merging stderr into CSV can corrupt it.
exercise.solution: Write report rows to stdout or a report file. Send diagnostics to stderr or a separate log. Diagnostic text does not satisfy the report schema and must not enter its data stream.
checks: Send report data to stdout or its file and diagnostics to stderr or a log.
Explain how a diagnostic line would violate the CSV schema if streams were merged.

quiz.question: An importer emits CSV plus a validation message. How should those outputs be routed?
options: CSV to the data stream and diagnostics to a separate error stream
Both to stdout so the CSV consumer can infer which lines are errors
Both to stderr so every line is treated as diagnostic evidence
quiz.explanation: Send CSV to stdout and the validation message to stderr. Mixing the message into stdout can make the downstream CSV reader interpret it as a data row.

lessons.title: 6. Search and transform text with pipelines
lessons.takeaway: Small tools joined by pipes answer most log and file questions; quote patterns and pass file names with NUL separators.

sections.title: Filters that do one job
paragraphs: Most text tools read lines from files or standard input and write lines to standard output, so they can be joined with `|`. `grep` selects lines that match a pattern (`-c` counts them, `-l` lists matching files, `-v` inverts, `-E` enables extended regular expressions). `cut` takes fields by a delimiter, `sort` orders lines (`-n` numerically, `-r` reversed, `-k` by field), and `uniq -c` counts runs of identical adjacent lines, which is why it almost always follows `sort`.

`awk` splits each line into fields `$1`, `$2` and so on, and runs a pattern-and-action program: `$4 >= 500 {n++}` counts lines whose fourth field is at least 500, and an `END` block runs after the last line, where `NR` holds the number of lines read. `sed` edits a stream: `s/old/new/` substitutes, `-E` enables extended regular expressions, and `-i` edits a file in place.
Put patterns and programs in single quotes so the shell passes `$4` and `*` to the tool instead of expanding them itself, as lesson 4 explained.

sections.title: Counting failures in an access log
paragraphs: The log has five requests. `grep -c` counts the two failures. `awk | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` builds a frequency table of method and path. `awk` with a numeric comparison counts errors without a regular expression, and `sed` strips the `ms` suffix so `awk` can average the durations. The last pipeline prints the timestamps of failed `GET /orders` requests.
These outputs were produced with GNU grep, sed and awk. BSD and macOS versions differ in some options, such as `sed -i` needing an explicit suffix argument.
sections.example:
cat > access.log <<'EOF'
2026-11-08T10:00:01 GET /orders 200 12ms
2026-11-08T10:00:02 GET /orders 500 40ms
2026-11-08T10:00:03 POST /orders 201 30ms
2026-11-08T10:00:04 GET /health 200 1ms
2026-11-08T10:00:05 GET /orders 500 38ms
EOF
grep -c ' 500 ' access.log
# 2
awk '{print $2, $3}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
#       3 GET /orders
#       1 POST /orders
#       1 GET /health
awk '$4 >= 500 {n++} END {print n " errors of " NR " requests"}' access.log
# 2 errors of 5 requests
sed -E 's/([0-9]+)ms$/\1/' access.log | awk '{sum += $5} END {printf "mean %.1f ms\n", sum / NR}'
# mean 24.2 ms
grep -E '^[^ ]+ GET /orders 5[0-9]{2} ' access.log | cut -d' ' -f1
# 2026-11-08T10:00:02
# 2026-11-08T10:00:05

sections.title: File names, find and xargs
paragraphs: `find` walks a directory tree and tests each entry: `-type f`, `-name '*.log'`, `-mtime +7` (modified more than seven days ago), `-size +100M`. It can run a command itself with `-exec cmd {} +`, or pass names to `xargs`, which builds command lines from its input.

By default `xargs` splits its input on spaces and newlines, so a file named `day one.log` becomes two arguments. `find -print0` with `xargs -0` separates names with a NUL byte, which cannot appear in a file name, and keeps every name intact. The first command below finds the failing log; the second, without NUL separators, breaks the name in two.
`sed -i` rewrites a file. Keep a backup suffix (`-i.bak`) or work on a copy until the expression is proven, and test the command without `-i` first so its output appears on screen.
sections.example:
mkdir -p logs/old
cp access.log "logs/old/day one.log"
printf 'nothing failed\n' > logs/today.log
find logs -type f -name '*.log' -print0 | xargs -0 grep -l ' 500 '
# logs/old/day one.log
find logs -type f -name '*.log' | xargs grep -l ' 500 '
# grep: logs/old/day: No such file or directory
# grep: one.log: No such file or directory

printf 'host=old.example.test\nport=80\n' > app.conf
sed -i.bak 's/^host=.*/host=new.example.test/' app.conf
cat app.conf
# host=new.example.test
# port=80
ls app.conf*
# app.conf
# app.conf.bak

exercise.prompt: Using access.log from the lesson, print each path with its number of 500 responses, most frequent first, and only for paths that had at least one. Then explain why `sort` must come before `uniq -c`.
exercise.solution:
awk '$4 == 500 {print $3}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
#       2 /orders
checks: Only /orders appears, with a count of 2.
awk filters on the status field instead of matching 500 anywhere in the line, such as in a duration.
uniq -c counts adjacent duplicates only, so unsorted input would split the same path into several counts.

quiz.question: A script runs `find . -name '*.log' | xargs rm` and one file is called `old report.log`. What happens to it?
options: It is removed normally
rm receives `./old` and `report.log` as two names and fails to remove it
find skips names containing spaces
quiz.explanation: xargs splits its input on blanks by default. Use find -print0 with xargs -0, or find -exec rm {} +, to keep each name as one argument.

lessons.title: 7. Users, groups and permission bits
lessons.takeaway: Each process has identities used in access decisions.

sections.title: Identity and directory permissions
paragraphs: Each process has identities used in access decisions. Traditional file mode bits separate owner, group and others with read, write and execute permissions. For a directory, execute allows traversal, read lists names, and write concerns entries. ACLs and capabilities add rules beyond the basic bits.

sections.title: Mode 600 and parent traversal
paragraphs: A private report can use mode 600: owner read/write, no group/other bits. An application still needs traversal permission on every parent directory. Fixing the final file alone may leave Permission denied unchanged.
sections.example:
# Linux lab only, own file:
chmod 600 backup.csv
ls -l backup.csv
id
# Expect owner rw bits, plus your actual identity.

sections.title: Diagnosing denied access
paragraphs: chmod 777 is not a diagnosis. An effective identity, parent access, ACL, mount option or security policy can explain a failure. Windows NTFS permissions and WSL-mounted directories may behave differently.

sections.title: Build each permission digit
paragraphs: Read has value 4, write 2 and execute 1. Add the required values separately for owner, group and others. Thus 6 means read plus write, 5 means read plus execute, and 0 means none. The three digits in 640 therefore describe rw-, r-- and ---. Directory traversal still needs the directory execute bit; these digits do not replace that separate check.
sections.example:
600 = owner 4+2, group 0, others 0
750 = owner 4+2+1, group 4+1, others 0

exercise.prompt: Decode 640 and explain why a readable file inside a non-traversable parent remains inaccessible.
exercise.solution: 640 grants owner read/write and group read. Directory traversal is a separate requirement, so access can fail before the file is reached.
checks: Decode 640 as owner read/write, group read and no access for others.
Identify missing parent-directory traversal as a separate reason file access can fail.

quiz.question: A user has read permission on a file but no traversal permission on its parent. What explains the failed read?
options: The path cannot be traversed to reach the readable file
File read permission must always include file write permission
The file must have execute permission before its bytes can be read
quiz.explanation: The process needs permission to traverse the parent directories as well as permission to read the file. File read permission alone cannot make an inaccessible path reachable.

lessons.title: 8. Processes and exit status
lessons.takeaway: A process is an executing program with a PID, resources and execution state.

sections.title: Process identity and exit status
paragraphs: A process is an executing program with a PID, resources and execution state. Its parent launches it and eventually collects completion status. A conventional zero status indicates success; nonzero statuses communicate failure categories. Program-specific documentation defines their meanings.

sections.title: Validation failure with exit 1
paragraphs: The importer prints a helpful message but exits 1 when validation fails. Automation should inspect the exit status as well as output. A shell command not found is different from an application rejecting input.
sections.example:
python3 -c 'import sys; print("rejected", file=sys.stderr); sys.exit(1)'
printf "status=%s\n" "$?"
ps -p $$ -o pid,ppid,comm
# First status is 1; the shell PID varies.

sections.title: PID reuse and effect evidence
paragraphs: PIDs are reusable. Do not act on an old PID without confirming identity. A status alone does not prove a business effect was rolled back; transaction design establishes that guarantee.

exercise.prompt: Define success and invalid-input exit statuses for a CLI, then identify which stream should carry the failure explanation.
exercise.solution: Use 0 for completed work and a documented nonzero value for invalid input. Send a useful explanation to stderr and avoid claiming output was committed.
checks: Assign 0 to success and a documented nonzero value to invalid input.
Send the failure explanation to stderr without claiming an output commit.

quiz.question: An importer rejects invalid input after printing a helpful explanation. What should automation use to detect the failure?
options: A documented nonzero exit status together with the diagnostic
The presence of any printed text as proof of failure
A zero exit status because the error was handled intentionally
quiz.explanation: Automation uses the documented nonzero exit status to detect failure. The diagnostic explains the cause; printing a helpful message does not change a successful exit status into a failure.

lessons.title: 9. Environment, PATH and configuration
lessons.takeaway: A child normally inherits an environment snapshot from its parent.

sections.title: Inherited configuration and PATH
paragraphs: A child normally inherits an environment snapshot from its parent. PATH lists directories searched for command names. Environment variables are strings; applications must validate them. Working directory, interpreter version and explicit configuration together explain many laptop-versus-service differences.

sections.title: A different Python interpreter
paragraphs: A service might find a different python than your interactive shell. Record the absolute interpreter path and configuration source. A DATABASE_URL in an environment is configuration, but still sensitive and should not be printed into a troubleshooting report.
sections.example:
command -v python3
printf "%s\n" "$PATH"
NOTEBOOK_MODE=practice python3 -c 'import os; print(os.environ["NOTEBOOK_MODE"])'
# Expect practice, without permanent shell modification.

sections.title: Running children and secret exposure
paragraphs: Changing a variable in one shell does not retroactively update already-running children. Avoid placing untrusted directories at the front of PATH and do not include secrets in committed .env files.

exercise.prompt: List three facts to capture when a scheduled command works interactively but fails as a service.
exercise.solution: Record the effective user, the absolute executable path and its version, the working directory, and the configuration source. Redact secret values.
checks: Capture effective user, absolute executable and version, and working directory or configuration source.
Redact secret configuration values from the comparison.

quiz.question: A parent shell changes a variable after starting a child. What does the running child normally see?
options: Its inherited environment snapshot unless it changes its own value
The new parent value immediately through shared environment memory
The new value only when its PATH contains the parent shell
quiz.explanation: A child normally inherits a snapshot when it starts. Changing a variable in the parent shell does not retroactively change the running child environment; PATH is an executable-search setting, not a synchronization mechanism.

lessons.title: 10. Write shell scripts that fail safely
lessons.takeaway: Start with strict mode, quote every expansion, check arguments, clean up with trap and return meaningful exit codes.

sections.title: Strict mode, tests and loops
paragraphs: A script is a file of commands with a first line naming its interpreter, such as `#!/usr/bin/env bash`, and the execute permission from lesson 7. By default Bash keeps going after a failed command and treats an unset variable as empty, so a mistake in line 3 can make line 30 delete the wrong directory.

`set -e` exits when a command fails, except where the failure is being tested, such as in an `if` condition or before `||`. `set -u` makes an unset variable an error. `set -o pipefail` gives a pipeline the status of its last failing command instead of only the last command. Together, `set -euo pipefail` is a common first line, but it is not a substitute for checking the cases you expect.

`[[ ... ]]` tests strings, numbers (`-eq`, `-lt`) and files (`-d` directory, `-f` regular file, `-e` exists). `for file in "$dir"/*.csv` loops over a glob; if nothing matches, Bash leaves the pattern itself, so check that the file exists. `$((...))` does integer arithmetic. Functions group commands and read their arguments as `$1`, `$2` and `"$@"`.

Exit codes are the script's contract with its caller: 0 for success, 1 for a failure in the work, 2 for incorrect usage is a common convention. Error messages go to standard error with `>&2`, so a caller can capture the real output separately.

sections.title: A CSV line counter
paragraphs: `count-lines.sh` checks it has exactly one argument, checks that it is a directory, and uses a temporary file that `trap ... EXIT` removes however the script ends. It quotes every expansion, so `q1 report.csv` stays one file name. `${file##*/}` removes the directory part, like `basename`.
The three runs show the three exit codes: 0 with a report, 1 for a missing directory, and 2 with a usage message when the argument is missing.
sections.example:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Report the line count of each CSV file in a directory, largest first.
set -euo pipefail

usage() { echo "usage: ${0##*/} DIRECTORY" >&2; exit 2; }
[[ $# -eq 1 ]] || usage
dir=$1
[[ -d $dir ]] || { echo "not a directory: $dir" >&2; exit 1; }

tmp=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT

count=0
for file in "$dir"/*.csv; do
  [[ -e $file ]] || continue            # the glob matched nothing
  lines=$(wc -l < "$file")
  printf '%s\t%s\n' "$lines" "${file##*/}" >> "$tmp"
  count=$((count + 1))
done
sort -rn "$tmp"
echo "files: $count"

./count-lines.sh data; echo "status $?"
# 3	q1 report.csv
# 1	q2.csv
# files: 2
# status 0
./count-lines.sh missing; echo "status $?"
# not a directory: missing
# status 1
./count-lines.sh; echo "status $?"
# usage: count-lines.sh DIRECTORY
# status 2

sections.title: What strict mode does and does not catch
paragraphs: Without `pipefail`, `false | true` succeeds because only the last command's status counts. `set -u` stops at the first unset variable with status 127 in this Bash, before the next line runs. A failing command used as an `if` condition does not trigger `set -e`, which is what makes `if grep -q` safe.

`set -e` has surprising exceptions: it is ignored inside functions called from an `if` or `||`, and a failing command substitution inside `local var=$(cmd)` is masked by `local` itself succeeding. Check important results explicitly, and run ShellCheck, a static analyser that catches unquoted expansions and these traps.
When logic grows to data structures, error recovery or more than a page, move it to Python or another language with real error handling, and keep the shell script as a thin launcher.
sections.example:
bash -c 'false | true; echo "without pipefail: $?"'
# without pipefail: 0
bash -c 'set -o pipefail; false | true; echo "with pipefail: $?"'
# with pipefail: 1
bash -c 'set -u; echo "name=$NAME"; echo unreachable'; echo "status $?"
# bash: line 1: NAME: unbound variable
# status 127
bash -c 'set -e; if grep -q x /dev/null; then echo found; else echo "no match, still running"; fi'
# no match, still running

exercise.prompt: Write a script `archive-old.sh DIR DAYS` that lists `.log` files in DIR older than DAYS days, one per line, safely for names with spaces. It must exit 2 with a usage message if the arguments are wrong, and 1 if DIR is not a directory or DAYS is not a whole number.
checks: Wrong argument count prints usage to stderr and exits 2.
A missing directory or a non-numeric DAYS exits 1 with a message on stderr.
find -print0 with read -d '' keeps names containing spaces intact.
Every expansion is quoted, including "$dir" and "$days".

quiz.question: A script uses set -e. Which failing command does NOT stop it?
options: `cp a b` on a line of its own
`grep -q x file` used as an `if` condition
`cd /missing` on a line of its own
quiz.explanation: set -e ignores failures in commands that are being tested, such as an if condition or the left side of || and &&.

lessons.title: 11. Launch, wait and time out
lessons.takeaway: A parent must manage child completion, bounded output and cleanup.

sections.title: Child lifetime and timeout
paragraphs: A parent must manage child completion, bounded output and cleanup. Waiting indefinitely can stall a workflow. A timeout is a local deadline; terminating one process does not necessarily terminate grandchildren. Argument lists and controlled executable paths reduce shell-related surprises.

sections.title: Successful and timed-out children
paragraphs: Run a child that prints 42 and then a child that sleeps. The supplied portable lab uses `subprocess.run` with a timeout and tests the resulting `TimeoutExpired`. It launches only the current Python interpreter and never scans or kills unrelated processes.
sections.example:
import subprocess, sys
result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", "print(42)"],
                        capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=2)
print(result.returncode, result.stdout.strip())
# Expected: 0 42

sections.title: Direct-child and output limits
paragraphs: The portable lab verifies direct-child behavior, not Linux process groups or a production supervisor. Output capture in memory needs a bound for potentially large output. For streaming tools consume output incrementally.

sections.title: Inspect one trusted child first
paragraphs: The returned `CompletedProcess` keeps `returncode`, `stdout` and `stderr` separate. A nonzero child status does not raise automatically with the default `check=False`. A timeout raises `TimeoutExpired` instead of returning a normal completion. Start with these two observable outcomes before designing a supervisor for descendants.

exercise.prompt: Replace the child source string "print(42)" with "import sys; print('bad row', file=sys.stderr); sys.exit(2)". Predict returncode, stdout and stderr, then run it with the same argument list and timeout. How does this differ from TimeoutExpired?
exercise.solution: The result has returncode 2, empty stdout and stderr "bad row\n". subprocess.run returns normally because check=True was not requested. TimeoutExpired is an exception when the child exceeds the wait; it is not status 2. Optional later extension: study descendant cleanup and output limits after resource-limits.
checks: Keep child status distinct from the parent exception.
Use only the fixed trusted snippet and the existing current-interpreter argument list.

quiz.question: A timed-out tool spawned grandchildren and produced large output. What is still needed beyond a direct-child timeout?
options: A descendant cleanup policy and explicit output/resource bounds
Only a longer timeout so the grandchildren can finish
Unbounded in-memory capture so no diagnostic output is lost
quiz.explanation: Use an appropriate OS sandbox/supervisor, resource limits, process-group cleanup and bounded streaming output; a single run timeout alone is insufficient.

lessons.title: 12. Graceful shutdown and signals
lessons.takeaway: A signal is an OS notification to a process or thread.

sections.title: Signals and bounded shutdown
paragraphs: A signal is an OS notification to a process or thread. A service can respond to a termination request by stopping new work, finishing or cancelling bounded work, flushing state and exiting. SIGKILL cannot be caught, so cleanup must tolerate interruption.

sections.title: A 30-second shutdown budget
paragraphs: A worker with a 30-second shutdown budget should stop accepting tasks first, allow current work up to the remaining deadline, then record incomplete tasks for retry. Signal handlers should do minimal safe work; ordinary cleanup can happen in the main execution flow.
sections.example:
# Linux observation of your own shell process only:
ps -p $$ -o pid,stat,comm
# Design note: SIGTERM requests shutdown; SIGKILL prevents cleanup.

sections.title: Actions limited to owned processes
paragraphs: Signals differ on Windows. Never send kill commands to arbitrary PIDs in this notebook. The Linux observation guide restricts actions to a process that you launched in a disposable user session.

exercise.prompt: Sketch shutdown when one task finishes and a second exceeds the deadline. Which state must survive abrupt termination?
exercise.solution: Stop accepting new work and finish the task that fits within the shutdown deadline. Save unfinished work durably for retry. Durable work identity must survive a process that cannot run cleanup.
checks: Stop intake and complete only work that fits the shutdown deadline.
Keep unfinished work identity durable so retry remains possible without cleanup.

quiz.question: A worker receives SIGKILL before its cleanup code runs. Which recovery assumption is valid?
options: SIGKILL cannot be caught, so unfinished work identity must already be durable
A finally block will always save unfinished work before termination
A termination handler can extend the deadline after SIGKILL
quiz.explanation: SIGKILL cannot be caught or handled by cleanup code. Any information needed to recover unfinished work must already have been saved durably before that signal arrives.

lessons.title: 13. Virtual memory and resident memory
lessons.takeaway: Each process works with a virtual address space.

sections.title: Virtual and resident memory
paragraphs: Each process works with a virtual address space. Mappings may refer to physical pages, shared libraries or files; reserved address space is different from resident physical memory. Page faults can bring data into memory or report invalid access. Resident memory and virtual size answer different questions.

sections.title: Mapping a large file
paragraphs: A process maps a large file but touches only a small part. Virtual size can be large while resident memory stays lower. Conversely, a growing Python list can increase resident usage. Diagnose trends alongside workload rather than comparing one number to a different metric.
sections.example:
# Linux read-only observation:
ps -p $$ -o pid,vsz,rss,comm
# VSZ and RSS typically appear in KiB; confirm your ps manual.

sections.title: Container accounting limits
paragraphs: A memory limit applies in a resource-accounting context. Host free memory does not imply a constrained container can allocate more. The course does not induce out-of-memory failures on your PC.

exercise.prompt: Explain why VSZ=2 GiB and RSS=120 MiB is not evidence of a 2 GiB physical leak.
exercise.solution: VSZ includes reserved and mapped virtual address space. Track resident memory and heap growth under an equivalent workload, then inspect allocations before calling the growth a leak.
checks: Distinguish the 2 GiB virtual mapping from the 120 MiB resident measurement.
Request resident or heap trends under equivalent workload before diagnosing a leak.

quiz.question: A process shows VSZ 2 GiB and RSS 120 MiB. What can you conclude from these values alone?
options: Virtual address space differs from current resident use; a leak is not established
The process is consuming 2 GiB of physical RAM
The 120 MiB RSS proves that no allocation leak can exist
quiz.explanation: VSZ measures virtual address space, while RSS measures memory currently resident in RAM. These two values alone do not show that the process is leaking memory; investigate how retained memory changes over time.

lessons.title: 14. Threads, scheduling and shared state
lessons.takeaway: Threads within a process share resources such as address space but have separate execution contexts.

sections.title: Interleaving and shared state
paragraphs: Threads within a process share resources such as address space but have separate execution contexts. Scheduling can interleave operations. A read-modify-write sequence is not automatically atomic, and more workers can increase contention rather than useful throughput.

sections.title: A lost increment
paragraphs: Two workers both read `count=5` and both write 6. One increment is lost. A lock around the full read-modify-write operation can prevent this race within a process. Separate processes need coordination that they can both access; an in-process lock cannot coordinate them.
sections.example:
# Conceptual interleaving, not runnable code:
worker A: read 5
worker B: read 5
worker A: write 6
worker B: write 6
# Intended total: 7; observed total: 6

sections.title: Runtime locks and workload models
paragraphs: A language runtime lock is not a complete application correctness guarantee. CPU-bound and I/O-bound workloads benefit from different models. Measure useful throughput and tail latency with a fixed workload.

exercise.prompt: State the smallest critical section needed to preserve count += 1 and why locking just the final write fails.
exercise.solution: Protect the read, calculation and write with the same lock. Locking only the write lets both workers calculate the same next value from stale reads.
checks: Protect the read, calculation and write as one critical section.
Show how both workers can compute 6 from 5 when only final writes are locked.

quiz.question: Two workers read count=5 and each writes 6. Which locking boundary preserves both increments?
options: One lock covering read, calculation and write
A lock covering only each final write
A lock covering only the printed result
quiz.explanation: The lock must cover the whole read-modify-write operation. Locking only the write still lets both workers calculate 6 from the same old value of 5.

lessons.title: 15. File descriptors and resource lifetimes
lessons.takeaway: A descriptor is a process-local handle to an open resource.

sections.title: Open handles and unlinked files
paragraphs: A descriptor is a process-local handle to an open resource. Multiple descriptors can refer to the same underlying open file description. Opening many files without closing them eventually exhausts a limit. Closing resources promptly is a correctness concern as well as a performance concern.

sections.title: Closing an unlinked file
paragraphs: Use a with block around a report file so normal completion and exceptions both close it. A Linux process may continue reading an open file after its pathname is unlinked; the name and the open object have distinct lifetimes.
sections.example:
from pathlib import Path
with Path("backup.csv").open(encoding="utf-8") as stream:
    print(stream.readline().strip())
print(stream.closed)
# Expected: "id,name" then True

sections.title: Reclaiming space and closing resources
paragraphs: Removing a log pathname does not necessarily reclaim disk usage while a process holds it open. Never delete active logs to diagnose a production server. A context manager closes handles but does not guarantee committed business data.

sections.title: Observe EMFILE without changing the shell limit
paragraphs: A process can run out of descriptors even when disk space and memory remain available. EMFILE names the per-process descriptor boundary; ENFILE is a different system-wide open-file-table boundary. Repeatedly reopening a harmless file such as /dev/null can demonstrate exhaustion without corrupting its content. Raising a limit merely moves the failure if handles still accumulate.

The optional `linux_fd_drill.py` starts a child with a small `RLIMIT_NOFILE`, opens descriptors until Linux returns `EMFILE`, closes every opened descriptor in `finally`, and proves a new open succeeds. The parent and shell limits are untouched. `/proc/self/fd` counts can include the directory handle used to inspect them, so compare observations made in the same way instead of expecting an absolute number across machines.
sections.example:
child only: soft RLIMIT_NOFILE=32
repeated open -> OSError(errno.EMFILE)
close owned descriptors -> count returns to baseline
new open -> succeeds

exercise.prompt: Run python3 linux_fd_drill.py in an existing Linux/WSL distribution. Explain why freeing disk space would not fix this injected failure and why successful reopening after cleanup matters.
checks: The child catches EMFILE and restores its descriptor count to the baseline.
A fresh open succeeds after closing handles; no shell or parent limit was changed.
exercise.solution: The failure concerns process handles, not allocated disk blocks. Recovery after close demonstrates that releasing the exhausted resource restores service. The exact count depends on inherited handles, so the checks compare before/after and the errno rather than hardcoding how many opens must succeed.

quiz.question: Repeated file opens eventually fail after many successes. What change addresses a possible descriptor leak?
options: Close handles on success and exception paths
Unlink each filename after opening it to close the descriptor
Increase the descriptor limit without checking resource lifetimes
quiz.explanation: Unclosed handles accumulate until the per-process/system resource limit is reached; inspect lifetime and count as well as the failing filename.

lessons.title: 16. Filesystems, caching and durability
lessons.takeaway: Writing data may update userspace buffers, kernel caches and finally storage at different times.

sections.title: Atomic replacement and durability
paragraphs: Writing data may update userspace buffers, kernel caches and finally storage at different times. Atomic rename/replacement changes which complete object a name refers to; durability concerns survival after a crash or power loss. These are separate properties.

sections.title: A temporary-file report writer
paragraphs: A report writer creates a temporary file in the same directory, writes and flushes it, synchronizes file contents and replaces the prior name. This prevents a reader from observing a half-written report under the stated filesystem assumptions. Full durability may also require directory synchronization and storage guarantees.
sections.example:
# Design sketch, not a crash-durability proof:
write temporary in target directory
flush application buffer; fsync temporary
replace target name
# Directory durability requires platform-specific consideration.

sections.title: Filesystem and storage assumptions
paragraphs: Cross-filesystem moves need not have atomic rename semantics. Network filesystems and hardware caches change assumptions. The practice lab does not certify power-loss behavior or concurrent writers.

exercise.prompt: Classify partial-write prevention, concurrent-writer serialization and power-loss survival as three separate requirements.
exercise.solution: Replacement can prevent partial visibility; locking/transactions coordinate writers; fsync and filesystem/storage policies address durability. No one operation establishes all three.
checks: Match complete-file visibility to replacement and writer coordination to locks or transactions.
Treat power-loss survival as a separate synchronization and storage guarantee.

quiz.question: A writer atomically replaces a report file. Which guarantee still needs separate evidence?
options: Survival after power loss under the filesystem and storage policy
Readers observing either the old or new complete file under the stated replacement assumptions
The pathname switching to the new file after successful replacement
quiz.explanation: Atomic replacement prevents readers from seeing a partly replaced file under the relevant filesystem rules. Survival after power loss also depends on flushing, filesystem and storage guarantees and needs separate verification.

lessons.title: 17. Inspect listeners and connections
lessons.takeaway: A network service binds an address and port.

sections.title: Listeners and reachability
paragraphs: A network service binds an address and port. Loopback accepts local communication; a wildcard bind may expose the service on available interfaces. Connection failures can arise from resolution, routing, filtering, listener state or application protocol.

sections.title: Reaching a local notebook server
paragraphs: A local notebook server on 127.0.0.1 is reachable only on that computer through loopback. A phone needs a reachable host address and appropriate network policy. First establish whether the expected process is listening before changing the application.
sections.example:
# Linux read-only inspection:
ss -ltn
# Look for the exact local port you deliberately started.
# -l listeners; -t TCP; -n numeric addresses.

sections.title: HTTP health beyond listening
paragraphs: Listening is not proof of a healthy HTTP response, TLS configuration or authorization. Do not expose practice services to public networks. ss availability and output fields vary by Linux environment.

exercise.prompt: Order checks for a refused local connection: hostname, listener, HTTP response, business authorization.
exercise.solution: Confirm the resolved destination and exact listener, then test the protocol response and business authorization separately. Refused connection occurs before HTTP authorization.
checks: Check the resolved destination and listener before HTTP response and business authorization.
Locate connection refusal before application-level authorization.

quiz.question: A process is listening on the expected port. Which further check is needed before claiming the application is healthy?
options: Check its protocol response and required application behavior
Treat the listener as proof that authentication succeeds
Treat the port number as proof that TLS is configured
quiz.explanation: A listening port shows that a socket is accepting connections. Check the protocol response and the required application operation before calling the service healthy.

lessons.title: 18. Services and supervision
lessons.takeaway: A supervisor starts a long-running process and manages its lifecycle.

sections.title: Supervisor configuration and readiness
paragraphs: A supervisor starts a long-running process and manages its lifecycle. On many Linux distributions systemd units describe the executable, identity, working directory, dependencies and restart policy. A running process is distinct from an application ready to accept work.

sections.title: A failing importer unit
paragraphs: An importer service repeatedly exits because its working directory differs from a terminal. Inspect unit configuration, current state and recent logs together. Restarting indefinitely without fixing an input/configuration failure can create a noisy loop.
sections.example:
# Linux with systemd, read-only:
systemctl --user --failed
# No user manager? Record that limitation; do not use sudo as a workaround.

sections.title: Unavailable service managers
paragraphs: WSL and containers may not run systemd as PID 1. Commands are observational and can fail with an explanatory unavailable message. Do not edit or enable system units as part of this notebook.

exercise.prompt: Specify executable, identity, working directory and restart conditions for a practice importer. Which failures should not retry rapidly?
exercise.solution: Use an absolute executable, unprivileged account and explicit working directory. If the configuration is permanently invalid, stop the service and alert its owner instead of restarting it repeatedly.
checks: Specify an absolute executable, unprivileged identity and explicit working directory.
Stop or alert on permanent invalid configuration instead of rapidly restarting it.

quiz.question: A supervisor reports a process running. What does this establish about readiness?
options: Lifecycle state is known; application readiness needs its own check
The application can already serve every required request
Its configuration is valid because the executable started
quiz.explanation: A supervisor can establish that a process started or is running. Readiness requires separate evidence that the application can perform its required work; a running process can still have missing dependencies or invalid configuration.

lessons.title: 19. Work remotely, copy files and schedule jobs
lessons.takeaway: Use SSH keys and host verification for access, rsync or tar for copies, and a scheduler that records failures.

sections.title: SSH keys and host verification
paragraphs: SSH authenticates in both directions. The server proves its identity with a host key: the first connection shows its fingerprint, and the client stores it in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. A changed host key on a later connection is a warning to investigate, not to bypass. Confirm a new fingerprint through another channel, such as the cloud console.

The user usually authenticates with a key pair. `ssh-keygen -t ed25519` creates a private key (keep it, protected by a passphrase) and a public key (copy it to the server's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, for example with `ssh-copy-id`). `ssh-agent` holds unlocked keys for a session. Password logins and root logins are commonly disabled on servers once keys work.

`~/.ssh/config` names hosts so commands stay short: a `Host` block can set `HostName`, `User`, `IdentityFile` and `ProxyJump` for reaching a private server through a bastion host. `ssh host 'command'` runs one command remotely and returns its exit status, which makes it usable in scripts.
sections.example:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "ada@laptop" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub ada@app1.example.test

# ~/.ssh/config
Host app1
    HostName app1.example.test
    User ada
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
    ProxyJump bastion.example.test

ssh app1 'systemctl is-active importer'   # prints active and exits 0 when the unit is running

sections.title: Copying and archiving
paragraphs: `scp` copies files over SSH. `rsync -a` copies a tree and, on later runs, sends only what changed, which suits repeated deployments and backups. A trailing slash matters: `rsync -a data/ host:/srv/data/` copies the contents of `data`, while `rsync -a data host:/srv/` creates `/srv/data`. `--dry-run` shows what would change, and `--delete` removes destination files missing from the source, so try it with `--dry-run` first.

`tar` bundles a tree into one file that keeps names, permissions and times. `-c` creates, `-x` extracts, `-t` lists, `-z` compresses with gzip, and `-C` changes directory first. Paths are stored as given, so archive from the parent directory to get relative paths. Listing before extracting an archive from elsewhere shows whether it would write outside the target.
The run below was made with GNU tar in a temporary directory: the archive lists relative paths, and extracting into `restore` recreates `data/a.csv` there.
sections.example:
cd /srv
tar -czf backup.tgz data
tar -tzf backup.tgz
# data/
# data/a.csv
mkdir restore && tar -xzf backup.tgz -C restore && cat restore/data/a.csv
# id
# 1

scp report.csv app1:/srv/reports/
rsync -a --dry-run --delete site/ app1:/srv/www/   # review, then run without --dry-run

sections.title: Scheduling with cron and systemd timers
paragraphs: A crontab line has five time fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week) and a command: `30 2 * * 1` means 02:30 every Monday, in the system's time zone. Cron starts commands with a minimal environment and `PATH`, from the user's home directory, so use absolute paths and redirect output to a log; otherwise output is mailed locally or discarded.

A systemd timer activates a service unit. `OnCalendar=Mon *-*-* 02:30:00` sets the schedule, and `Persistent=true` runs a missed job after the machine was off. The service's output goes to the journal (`journalctl -u backup.service`), its exit status is recorded, and `systemctl list-timers` shows the next and last run. Lesson 18 covered the service side.
Either way, a scheduled job should be safe to run twice, take a lock (for example `flock`) so a slow run does not overlap the next, and report failures to someone who will act on them.
sections.example:
# crontab -e : every Monday at 02:30, with a lock and a log
30 2 * * 1 /usr/bin/flock -n /run/lock/backup.lock /opt/backup/run.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1

# /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer
[Unit]
Description=Weekly backup

[Timer]
OnCalendar=Mon *-*-* 02:30:00
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

systemctl enable --now backup.timer
systemctl list-timers backup.timer

exercise.prompt: A nightly report script works when you run it by hand but produces nothing from cron. List the likely causes in order of what you would check, and rewrite the crontab line to make the next failure diagnosable.
exercise.solution:
1. Environment: cron's PATH is minimal, so commands such as python or aws may not be found. Use absolute paths or set PATH in the crontab.
2. Working directory: cron starts in the home directory, so relative paths such as data/input.csv resolve elsewhere.
3. Output: stdout and stderr were not captured, so the error was mailed locally or lost.
4. Permissions and identity: the job runs as the crontab's owner, which may lack access that your interactive shell had.
5. Schedule and time zone: confirm the five fields and the system time zone.

0 1 * * * cd /opt/report && /usr/bin/flock -n /run/lock/report.lock /opt/report/run.sh >> /var/log/report.log 2>&1
checks: Names the minimal environment and PATH as the first suspect.
Sets the working directory explicitly or uses absolute paths.
Redirects both stdout and stderr to a log the operator can read.
Mentions identity and the schedule's time zone.

quiz.question: Connecting to a known server, SSH warns that the host key has changed. What should you do first?

Confirm the new fingerprint through another trusted channel before trusting it
Disable StrictHostKeyChecking for that host
quiz.explanation: A changed host key can mean a rebuilt server or an interception. Verify the new fingerprint out of band before accepting it.

lessons.title: 20. Logs, clocks and incident evidence
lessons.takeaway: A useful incident record includes observation time, affected scope, exact command, relevant output and a testable hypothesis.

sections.title: Events, clocks and hypotheses
paragraphs: A useful incident record includes observation time, affected scope, exact command, relevant output and a testable hypothesis. Logs should identify events and correlation IDs without disclosing secrets. Wall-clock timestamps can jump; elapsed measurements should use a monotonic clock.

sections.title: A permission-denied timeline
paragraphs: A report says permission denied at 10:05. Record the service identity, path and parent modes before adjusting access. Test one change at a time so evidence can explain the result. Copy only necessary sanitized diagnostics into your learning notes.
sections.example:
import time
start = time.monotonic()
# perform bounded work
print(time.monotonic() - start)
# Nonnegative elapsed seconds; actual value varies.

sections.title: Missing evidence and originals
paragraphs: Absence of a log is not proof that an event did not occur. Buffered output, sampling, clock skew and unavailable storage can create gaps. Preserve originals and document transformations.

exercise.prompt: Write an evidence note for an importer failure without including the database password or entire customer file.
exercise.solution: Record the time with its timezone, the operation ID, a sanitized error category, the input schema and version, and the relevant path or identity. Keep sensitive source data only in approved storage.
checks: Include time and timezone, operation ID, sanitized error category, schema version and relevant path or identity.
Exclude the database password and complete customer file from the evidence note.

quiz.question: An importer fails and a teammate requests diagnostic evidence. Which response supports investigation?
options: Context and correlation metadata with secrets and customer records redacted
The full environment and input file so no context can be missing
Only the error sentence, omitting time, identity and operation details
quiz.explanation: Record the command, time, relevant error and correlation metadata so someone can reproduce or investigate the failure. Redact secrets and customer contents that are unnecessary for that investigation.

lessons.title: 21. Resource limits and overload
lessons.takeaway: Finite CPU, memory, handles and storage impose capacity limits.

sections.title: Arrival rate and capacity
paragraphs: Finite CPU, memory, handles and storage impose capacity limits. Queueing increases when arrivals exceed service capacity. Limits protect a host but can also make failures surprising if applications assume unrestricted resources. Capacity planning needs workload and concurrency assumptions.

sections.title: Backlog growing by 120 jobs
paragraphs: A worker processing 10 jobs/second receives 14/second for 30 seconds. Ignoring initial backlog and variance, backlog grows by 120 jobs. Increasing workers may help only if the bottleneck is parallelizable and downstream capacity permits it.
sections.example:
arrival = 14
service = 10
duration = 30
print(max(0, arrival - service) * duration)
# Expected: 120 queued jobs in a simplified constant-rate model.

sections.title: Bounded arithmetic practice
paragraphs: Do not stress your computer with unbounded allocations or fork loops. The provided lab is an arithmetic model and does not exercise kernel limits or reproduce load-test evidence.

exercise.prompt: Predict backlog after arrival returns to 8/second for 60 seconds. State the model assumptions.
exercise.solution: The worker has spare capacity of 2 jobs per second, so it clears 120 queued jobs in 60 seconds. This assumes constant rates, a service capacity of 10 jobs per second, no retries and equal job sizes.
checks: Calculate 2 jobs/second spare capacity and removal of the 120-job backlog in 60 seconds.
State constant rates, service capacity of 10, and no retries or job-size differences.

quiz.question: Arrival is 14 jobs/second and service is 10 for 30 seconds, starting empty. What is the modeled backlog?
options: 120 jobs, because arrivals exceed service by 4 each second
420 jobs, counting all arrivals without completed work
Zero jobs, because placing work in a queue increases service capacity
quiz.explanation: The queue grows by 14 minus 10 = 4 jobs per second. Over 30 seconds that adds 120 jobs, assuming an empty initial queue and constant rates. Queue storage does not increase service capacity.

lessons.title: 22. Containers through an OS lens
lessons.takeaway: Namespaces give processes distinct views of selected OS resources such as process IDs, mounts and networking.

sections.title: Resource views and accounting
paragraphs: Namespaces give processes distinct views of selected OS resources such as process IDs, mounts and networking. cgroups account for and constrain resource use. These mechanisms solve different problems; together with other controls they support container runtimes.

sections.title: PID and mount views
paragraphs: Inside a container, a process may see PID 1 while the host sees another PID. Its memory limit can be lower than host RAM. A missing file may come from a different mount view rather than a missing host file.
sections.example:
# Linux read-only observations; names and access vary:
cat /proc/self/cgroup
ls -l /proc/self/ns
# Compare observations, without modifying controls.

sections.title: Isolation and runtime policy
paragraphs: Isolation is not complete security by itself. Capabilities, user identities, seccomp, filesystem access and runtime policy still matter. This lesson uses read-only inspection; it does not create namespaces or change cgroup controls.

exercise.prompt: Match PID visibility and memory budget to their mechanisms. Explain why seeing PID 1 is not proof of host administrator access.
exercise.solution: A PID namespace controls which process IDs are visible. A memory cgroup controls the memory budget. A process ID alone establishes neither user identity nor capabilities.
checks: Match PID visibility to a PID namespace and memory budget to a cgroup.
Explain why PID 1 alone establishes neither host identity nor administrator capabilities.

quiz.question: A container sees PID 1 but has less memory available than the host. Which mechanisms explain these facts?
options: PID namespace for the view and a memory cgroup for the budget
The PID namespace sets both process numbering and the memory budget
The cgroup assigns PID 1 and grants host administrator identity
quiz.explanation: A PID namespace changes which process IDs the container sees. A memory cgroup limits its memory use. Seeing PID 1 inside the container does not grant host administrator access.

lessons.title: 23. Least privilege and package hygiene
lessons.takeaway: Least privilege grants only required operations to an application identity.

sections.title: Runtime permissions and packages
paragraphs: Least privilege grants only required operations to an application identity. Package management tracks installed software and updates; distributions have differing release policies and commands. Verify origin and compatibility before adding a dependency.

sections.title: A report reader's permissions
paragraphs: A report reader needs read access to input and write access to a dedicated output directory, not permission to modify executables. Separate deployment/configuration responsibilities from runtime rights. Record versions so a reproduction can explain environment differences.
sections.example:
# Observation only:
id
command -v python3
python3 --version
# Record distribution from /etc/os-release separately.

sections.title: Remote scripts and privilege
paragraphs: Piping a remote script into a privileged shell hides review and expands authority. Do not install packages or change users as part of this notebook; optional Linux exercises use an existing disposable VM/WSL environment.

exercise.prompt: Create a permission matrix for input CSV, report directory and application code.
exercise.solution: Runtime identity reads input, writes only reports and reads/executes installed code. It should not rewrite application code or obtain general administrator rights.
checks: Give the runtime read access to input, write access to reports and read/execute access to installed code.
Exclude application-code modification and general administrator rights.

quiz.question: A report importer reads CSV and writes reports. Which permission set matches its work?
options: Read input, write the report directory, and read/execute installed code
Write input and application code to simplify any future changes
Run as administrator to avoid diagnosing output-directory permissions
quiz.explanation: The importer needs to read input, write reports and read or execute its installed code. It does not need permission to modify its code or unrelated files.

lessons.title: 24. Diagnose a failed importer
lessons.takeaway: Start with a symptom and a bounded hypothesis rather than a broad fix.

sections.title: Lookup, access and validation failures
paragraphs: Start with a symptom and a bounded hypothesis rather than a broad fix. Separate executable lookup, configuration, file access, resource constraints and application validation. Prefer read-only evidence first, then a minimal reversible change in a practice environment.

sections.title: Locating a missing data.csv
paragraphs: If a service fails to open `data.csv`, compare working directory, absolute input path, identity and parent traversal. If it opens but rejects a row, inspect the schema error rather than changing OS permissions. The supplied diagnostic fixture models these categories portably.

sections.title: Simulation versus live diagnosis
paragraphs: A simulation trains reasoning but is not a real Linux incident investigation. Production diagnosis needs authorization, change records and safe evidence handling. The reference never reads arbitrary system files or changes permissions.

sections.title: Use errno to choose the next observation
paragraphs: An importer opens its first 29 files but cannot open the next one. The path exists and permissions are unchanged. If errno is EMFILE, inspect descriptor growth and handles left open after exceptions. Changing ownership will not release descriptors. If errno is ENOENT, inspect the absolute path and working directory. The message "cannot open file" alone does not identify the cause.

A minimal incident record keeps operation, errno, process identity and resource count with the timestamp. Avoid logging file contents to diagnose a resource boundary. Repeat one bounded operation after releasing the suspected handles, and verify the same process recovers. Restart can clear symptoms while hiding the leak; a regression test must also check cleanup on failed work.
sections.example:
same symptom: cannot open input
ENOENT -> resolve path/cwd
EACCES -> identity and parent traversal
EMFILE -> owned descriptor counts/lifetimes
valid open + ValueError -> schema/content category

exercise.prompt: The child descriptor drill fails with EMFILE, then succeeds after cleanup. An importer instead opens the file and rejects an amount. Give one discriminating observation and targeted fix for each.
checks: Use errno plus before/after descriptor counts for the open failure.
Use the validation field/category after a successful open for the rejected amount; permission changes are not the fix.
exercise.solution: For EMFILE, inspect resource lifetimes and close handles on all paths; prove recovery with a bounded reopen and count comparison. For the amount error, inspect schema and validation rules using a synthetic rejected value. The successful open already crossed the filesystem-access boundary; changing permissions would not validate the amount.

quiz.question: An importer opens the file but raises ValueError for an invalid amount. What should be inspected next?
options: The input schema and rejected-value category
The parent directory traversal bits before checking the value
Administrator privileges because all file-processing errors concern access
quiz.explanation: For a missing file, inspect the configured path and working directory. For an access failure, inspect the process identity, parent directories and access policy. For a timeout, inspect the deadline and process state. For a validation error, inspect the schema and rejected row category. A blanket sudo fix does not distinguish these causes.

lessons.takeaway: A portfolio should show reproducible observations, an explanation of mechanisms and a tested recovery procedure.

sections.title: Reproducible diagnosis and recovery
paragraphs: A portfolio should show reproducible observations, an explanation of mechanisms and a tested recovery procedure. sections.title: The final diagnostic case
paragraphs: The final case combines an explicit interpreter, validated configuration, a bounded child lifetime, correct output/error separation and an incident note. Evaluate whether your recovery addresses the cause and whether it preserves prior report data.

python -m unittest -v test_os_labs.py

sections.title: Completed Linux observations
paragraphs: Passing a portable suite does not prove scheduler knowledge, live service management, namespace isolation or performance under load. List the Linux observations you have actually completed and unanswered hypotheses.

exercise.prompt: Produce a one-page report with reproducible commands, failure timeline, safe fix and recovery verification.
exercise.solution: Include the tool and runtime versions, the exact bounded test, observations before and after recovery, and the state that was preserved. State which Linux and production behaviors remain untested.

Show preserved prior state and label modeled, executed and untested Linux behavior separately.

Linux service supervision is verified because both use processes
Production capacity is verified because each small test completed
quiz.explanation: The passing suite supports the portable behaviours it actually tested. Linux-specific mechanisms and production recovery still require their own observations and tests.
